extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science, philosophy of science, and inductive logic (e.g., scientists, philosophers, advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for establishing and testing causal laws by induction: four canonical experimental/inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues), plus joint methods, requirements for controls/repetition, and how to interpret residual phenomena and natural experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two cases identical in all material respects except the presence or absence of one antecedent; attribute difference in consequent to that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by experiments comparing corresponding limbs (one paralyzed, one healthy) of the same animal; requires assuming complete resemblance save one antecedent, which must be secured by repeating experiments often enough to exclude accidental differences. Used to prove causation directly (e.g., paralysis → greater irritability; cooling a surface → deposition of dew at some temperature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple instances agree only in one circumstantial antecedent, infer that this common circumstance is the cause (or part of the cause) of the observed consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the generalization 'dogs bark' from many dogs; cases of exhausted animals that agree only in preceding exhausting exercise which correlates with rapid putrefaction. The method establishes a connection by agreement but, by itself, is not sufficient to prove causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the degree or intensity of an antecedent varies along with corresponding variation in the consequent, infer that the antecedent is causally connected to the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when changes in magnitude correspond (e.g., more powerful galvanic charges shorten duration of cadaveric rigidity; degree of muscular irritability correlates with lateness/length of rigidity and rate of putrefaction). Can show dependence of effect on degree of antecedent; may play a subordinate role in complex investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate and subtract the effects of all known causes from an observed phenomenon; the remaining residual phenomena point to unknown causes deserving inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comet period residuals suggesting a resisting medium; unexplained retarding influence of copper on a vibrating needle (Arago); residual velocity in sound explained by heat development (Laplace); discovery of new chemical elements in concentrated residues. Requires that effects of known causes be estimated (ideally calculated) and subducted—failure to do so can misclassify the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine Agreement and Difference: identify instances that agree in a circumstance where the consequent occurs and instances where that circumstance is absent and the consequent does not occur, strengthening inductive inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown in the muscular-nutrition examples: cases of late/long rigidity agree only in high muscular nutrition, while opposite cases agree only in poor nutrition. Joint application narrows alternative explanations but, like Agreement alone, requires the aggregate antecedent's causal relation (established elsewhere) to prove particular causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural experiments (nature performs the Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When nature itself introduces a single, definite new circumstance and the consequent appears rapidly without other material changes, treat the instance as a natural Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a clear opening in the clouds during a night produces dew deposition quickly—because the change is single and rapid, it satisfies the Method of Difference. Useful for verifying phenomena on large scales that cannot be commanded experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive corroboration from known properties of agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduce the effect from ascertained properties of agents known to be present; use deduction to account for causation and exceptions before or alongside experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deducing dew formation from properties of aqueous vapor and surface cooling explains both causation and exceptions (e.g., no dew in very dry air). Deduction complements experiment by revealing additional necessary conditions not detected by other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to exclude accidental differences by repetition and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that compared cases differ only in the antecedent of interest must be tested by repeating experiments sufficiently often and controlling other conditions to exclude accidental or hidden differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comparison of paralysed and healthy limbs is valid only when repeated across different animals and with care to avoid accidental pathological differences; repeated replication secures the conditions of the Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating causation by showing effect follows regardless of how antecedent is produced
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the consequent follows whenever the antecedent is present, irrespective of the variety of causes that produce that antecedent, to ensure the effect depends on the antecedent itself rather than on its causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the muscular irritability case, irritability produced by paralysis, cold, or good nutrition all lead to the same retardation and prolongation of rigidity; since the effect follows from the irritability however caused, the irritability itself is the causal factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate known causes before assigning residual phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying the Method of Residues, known causes' effects should be estimated (ideally by calculation) and subducted from observed phenomena so that genuine residuals reveal new causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arago's needle-over-copper example would be a true Residues application only if the effects of air resistance and thread rigidity had been calculated a priori and subtracted; otherwise it is a Method of Difference example. Proper quantitative allowance is important for valid residual inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for exceptions and additional conditions in causal explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory causal theory should account for exceptions to general phenomena by identifying additional conditions that permit or prevent the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deductive proof of the dew theory identifies humidity as an additional necessary condition—explaining lack of dew in very dry weather. Accounting for exceptions increases the fullness and reliability of inductive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods as tests of induction (proof) distinct from methods of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The Four Methods primarily provide a test for inductive arguments (proof of inductions) rather than an exhaustive account of how discoveries are made; they serve as criteria to judge when inductive inferences are conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to Whewell's critique, the text argues that although the Methods may not directly generate hypotheses, they are essential for proving and validating inductions. They help judge correctness of inferences even when reduction to formal ABC/_abc_ is practically difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: Agreement and Joint Methods cannot alone prove causation without additional proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement and its Joint form, while suggestive, are defective in proving causation by themselves because agreement does not exclude common but non-causal associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that Agreement needs to be supplemented by Difference or other evidence (e.g., known causal relation of aggregate antecedent to consequent) to achieve proof. Historical and complex discoveries often require deduction alongside the methods of observation and experiment.
